text: 2-XL is an educational toy robot marketed from 1978 to 1981 by the Mego Corporation and from 1992 to 1995 by Tiger Electronics. It was the first "smart-toy" to exhibit rudimentary intelligence, memory, gameplay, and responsiveness, and was given a personality that kept children engaged through verbal interactions, jokes, and funny sayings. The toy was invented and patented by Michael J. Freeman, Ph.D., who also voiced the robot using a synthesizer to create a high-pitched robot-like sound, shaping its personality. First introduced in 1978 by Mego, a US-based toy company in New York City, 2-XL became a commercial success and was sold in multiple countries with tapes translated into seven foreign languages. It used 8-track tapes that presented multiple-choice questions, with users selecting answers via buttons that changed the tape's path, enabling interactive gameplay. The robot could respond verbally based on user input, and its personality was highlighted by lines such as "Perhaps your brain went on strike! You are Wrong" or "Nice try but (whispering) you are wrong, but go ahead, I will be a nice little toy robot and give you a second chance now." If correct, it praised the user with phrases like "You must be a genius. Good work" or "Nice answer, football is correct." The original 2-XL had a brown plastic body with white facial features, two red light bulbs for eyes that flashed during operation, four red buttons for answering questions, and a volume/power knob. It played up to two hours of content covering sports, the Guinness Book of World Records, the metric system, general knowledge, and jokes. A 1980 revision featured brighter red eyes that responded to voice, a glossier plastic finish, and a rounder speaker. A school-specific version included earphone jacks, curriculum tapes, and a teacher's manual. In 1992, Tiger Electronics re-introduced 2-XL with cassette tapes that were twice as long as the original 8-track tapes and offered better sound quality, using all four tracks of a cassette to create interactive audio responses. Freeman again recorded the voice in a professional studio, and the new version included a light-up circular mouth and a headphone jack, allowing it to run on batteries. The cassette version used the same interactive logic as the original, leveraging the four-track structure to provide different audio outputs based on button presses. This concept was inspired by the Talk 'n Play system and earlier home cassette recorders. New tapes featured popular characters and media such as Spider-Man, X-Men, Star Trek: The Next Generation, Power Rangers, Jurassic Park, Superman, and Batman, allowing users to make choices that influenced story outcomes, similar to Choose Your Own Adventure books. The second version was available from 1992 to 1996, with about 45 tapes released, sold internationally including in Japan, Germany, Hungary, Italy, France, the UK, Ireland, Canada, and Brazil (distributed by Playtronic), and translated into many languages—though not recorded by Freeman. The original version included a program called "The World of 2-XL" with each unit, while other programs were sold separately. One final Mego tape, "Trilex," was a board game with a pyramid-shaped board and four colored slots aligned with the robot’s buttons, enabling users to drop checkers that would press the corresponding track buttons, aiming to form lines or triangles of three checkers of the same color, simulating a game-playing AI. Secondary products under the 2-XL name included laptop bags, earphones, and lunch boxes. Both versions won numerous awards, including FamilyFun’s 1992 best toy award, Right Start Magazine’s 1993 Europe’s best toy for ages 3–5, and Playthings magazine’s 75th anniversary cover naming 2-XL one of the top ten toys of all time. The Tiger 2-XL also won the 1992 Walt Disney Company Best Learning Toy award. The toy's success also inspired a game show, Pick Your Brain, and it served as a spokesrobot for basketball player Michael Jordan and his foundation in 1992 and 1993, appearing in several public service announcements with him. The name "2-XL" is a pun on "to excel."
